drivers.title: Lukoil foreign assets up for sale
drivers.text: A US-led consortium led by Eldridge agreed to buy LUKOIL International, which holds upstream output of about 350,000 boe/d, three refineries and a trading arm. The price is paid in restricted Russian shares rather than cash, and the deal needs conditional OFAC approval.

sowhat.text: Large deals keep coming, from Sanofi's cash bid for Insmed to the Lukoil asset sale, which shows energy M&A now runs through sanctions approvals as much as price. With PCE inflation at 3.8% and the 10-year at 4.85%, acquirers financing with debt face a high base rate.

pitch: Wednesday was a choppy but contained day. Chip stocks sold off hard in the morning and recovered most of it, so the S&P 500 ended down about 0.3 percent near 7,180 and the Nasdaq down 0.6 percent. Data was strong: third-quarter GDP was revised up to 4.3 percent, but October PCE inflation was 3.8 percent, and the 10-year still eased to about 4.85 percent. Oil rose, with WTI up 2 percent to about 84 dollars and Brent up 3.5 percent to about 95. On deals, a US-led consortium agreed to buy Lukoil's international assets in a share swap that needs Treasury sign-off, and Sanofi's roughly 41 billion dollar cash deal for Insmed is still the biggest of the week.

quiz.q: Where did the 10-year Treasury close on Wed 25 Nov?
Why did the Nasdaq end down only 0.6% after a big drop early on 25 Nov?
quiz.a: Chipmakers led a morning sell-off, with Nvidia and Micron down sharply, but stocks recovered most of the loss by the close.

quiz.q: Who leads the consortium buying LUKOIL International, and how is it paying?
quiz.a: Eldridge leads it, paying with restricted Russian shares rather than cash.

chat.a: Wednesday was a recovery from an ugly morning: chips sold off hard, then the S&P 500 closed down only 0.3% at 7,183 and the Nasdaq down 0.6%. The Dow rose 0.3%. The VIX was 28.29 and the 10-year was 4.85%.
chat.tip: Lead with the intraday reversal, then give the levels.

chat.q: What's your read on oil this week?
chat.a: WTI settled at $83.68, up 2.0%, and Brent at $94.61, up 3.5%, a spread of about $11. Both have bounced two days in a row. For energy M&A, stable prices help buyers and sellers agree on value.
chat.tip: Give the level and direction, then stop.

chat.a: A US-led consortium led by Eldridge agreed to buy LUKOIL International, with Citi as lead financial adviser to the consortium. Sanofi agreed to buy Insmed for $175 a share in cash, about $41.0B, and CrowdStrike agreed to buy Zscaler for about $43.9B in stock. The last two releases did not name advisers.
chat.tip: Say the advisers were not disclosed rather than guess.

chat.q: What are you watching over the next couple of weeks?
chat.a: The Dec 4 jobs report and then the Dec 8-9 FOMC, with the funds rate at 3.75-4.00%. With PCE inflation at 3.8% and the 10-year at 4.85%, I want to see whether rates stay this high into year-end.
chat.tip: Tie each event to financing conditions.

chat.q: Why is the Lukoil deal structured as a share swap?
chat.a: The release says the consortium pays in restricted Russian shares, so no cash goes to Russia, and the sale consideration sits in a restricted account. It also needs conditional OFAC approval. The point for a banker is that sanctions approval and structure, not just price, decide whether the deal closes.
chat.tip: Say structure and approvals first, price second.

chat.q: If the 10-year rose 50 bp, what happens to a DCF?
chat.a: The 10-year is 4.85% now. A 50 bp rise lifts the risk-free rate and so the WACC, which lowers the present value of cash flows. Long-duration assets with most of their value in the terminal value are hit hardest.
chat.tip: Say the direction, then who is hit hardest.

chat.q: How would you describe credit markets right now?
chat.a: High yield was 372 bp and investment grade 98 bp on Tuesday, slightly wider than Monday. That is still a functioning market for acquisition financing, and Sanofi has committed debt financing for Insmed. Wednesday's reading is not yet published.
